title: Products of reduced affine varieties are reduced
statement:
Let $k$ be algebraically closed and let $X,Y$ be affine varieties over
$k$, with reduced finitely generated coordinate algebras $A=k[X]$ and
$B=k[Y]$. Then $A\otimes_kB$ is a reduced finitely generated
$k$-algebra, so $X\times Y=\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_kB)$ is an
affine variety whose $k$-points are the pairs $(x,y)$ of $k$-points.
In particular the vanishing principle of
[lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] applies to it: a regular
function on $X\times Y$ vanishing at all $k$-points $(x,y)$ is zero.
Thus an identity between regular maps defined on $X\times Y$ (such as a
commutator map) may be checked on $k$-points, one variable at a time.

proof.text: Choose finite algebra generators $a_1,\ldots,a_m$ of $A$ and $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ of $B$. The elements $a_i\otimes1$ and $1\otimes b_j$ generate $A\otimes_kB$ as a $k$-algebra: expand $a$ and $b$ as polynomials in the generators, then use $(a\otimes1)(1\otimes b)=a\otimes b$. Every tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors by the module tensor construction. Thus the displayed finite set generates every element, including when one algebra is the zero algebra or a generating set is empty.

source.place: first paragraph; Stacks 00F3 (definition-finite-type), 00CX (lemma-tensor-product), and 01I4 (lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes), universal-property calculation

proof.text: By the affine fibre-product formula, $X\times_kY=\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_kB)$. By the affine-spectrum morphism correspondence, a $k$-point is a ring map to $k$; functoriality identifies the condition that its morphism is over $\operatorname{Spec}k$ with compatibility with the structure map, precisely the $k$-algebra condition. Restricting $h:A\otimes_kB\to k$ along $a\mapsto a\otimes1$ and $b\mapsto1\otimes b$ gives a pair $(x,y)$. Conversely the algebra tensor universal property gives $h_{x,y}(a\otimes b)=x(a)y(b)$. Its uniqueness shows that these operations are inverse. Hence these are exactly the pairs of $k$-points, and this formula computes evaluation.

source.place: first paragraph; Stacks 01I4 (lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes), displayed Hom formula

proof.text: Choose a $k$-basis $(e_j)_{j\in J}$ of the vector space $B$, using the basis-existence clause of the cited node. Generation by pure tensors expresses an arbitrary nonzero $t$ as a finite linear combination; absorb each scalar into its first factor by $c(u\otimes v)=(cu)\otimes v$ to obtain a finite sum $\sum_{q=1}^m u_q\otimes v_q$. Expand each $v_q$ as a finite linear combination $\sum_{j\in J_0}c_{qj}e_j$, with a common finite index set $J_0$. Bilinearity gives $t=\sum_{j\in J_0}(\sum_qc_{qj}u_q)\otimes e_j$. Put $a_j=\sum_qc_{qj}u_q$. Some $a_j$ is nonzero, since otherwise this displayed expression is zero. The $e_j$ indexed by $J_0$ are linearly independent because they are distinct basis vectors. This proves the finite independent expansion used in the source; no finite-dimensionality of $A$ or $B$ is assumed.

source.place: second paragraph, the independent expansion; Stacks 00CX (lemma-tensor-product), construction by finite sums and bilinearity; basis existence as in the cited Mathlib leaf

proof.text:
Choose an index $j_0$ with $a_{j_0}
e0$. The contrapositive of clause (2) of the vanishing principle for the reduced finitely generated algebra $A$ gives a $k$-algebra map $x:A	o k$ with $x(a_{j_0})
e0$. The algebra tensor universal property with $a\mapsto x(a)1_B$ and $\mathrm{id}_B$ gives $E_x:A\otimes_kB	o B$, $a\otimes b\mapsto x(a)b$. Thus $E_x(t)=\sum_{j\in J_0}x(a_j)e_j$ is nonzero: if it were zero, linear independence would force every coefficient $x(a_j)$ to be zero, contradicting the chosen $j_0$. Applying the contrapositive of the same vanishing principle to the reduced finitely generated algebra $B$ gives $y:B	o k$ with $y(E_x(t))
e0$. The restrictions of $y\circ E_x$ along the two tensor inclusions are $a\mapsto y(x(a)1_B)=x(a)$ and $b\mapsto y(b)$, since $y$ is a $k$-algebra map. They equal the restrictions of $h_{x,y}$, so the algebra tensor uniqueness clause gives $y\circ E_x=h_{x,y}$. Therefore $t(x,y)
e0$. We have proved that every nonzero tensor is detected by a pair of rational points.

source.place: second paragraph, evaluation first in A and then in B

proof.text: If $t^r=0$ for an integer $r\ge1$, every evaluation homomorphism satisfies $h_{x,y}(t)^r=h_{x,y}(t^r)=0$. A field has no nonzero nilpotent: if $c\ne0$, multiplying $c^r=0$ by $(c^{-1})^r$ gives $1=0$. Thus every evaluation of $t$ is zero, and the detection result of the preceding step forces $t=0$. This proves reducedness. Together with steps 1 and 2 this makes $X\times_kY$ a reduced affine variety. The same detection result says directly that a regular function vanishing at every pair is zero. If a factor is empty (its algebra is zero), the tensor algebra is zero and these assertions are still valid.

source.place: third paragraph, nilpotence and the vanishing principle

proof.text: Let $Z=\operatorname{Spec}C$ be an affine variety, and let regular maps $\varphi,\psi:X\times_kY\to Z$ agree on every pair of $k$-points. For each $g\in C$, the element $d_g=\varphi^*(g)-\psi^*(g)$ satisfies $h_{x,y}(d_g)=(h_{x,y}\circ\varphi^*)(g)-(h_{x,y}\circ\psi^*)(g)=0$: functoriality of $\operatorname{Spec}$ identifies these composites with the coordinate maps of the equal points $\varphi(x,y)$ and $\psi(x,y)$. By the detection result proved in step 4, $d_g=0$. Consequently the two coordinate homomorphisms $C\to A\otimes_kB$ agree on every element; the uniqueness clause for morphisms between affine spectra gives $\varphi=\psi$. Checking the hypothesis one variable at a time is precisely proving $\forall x\,\forall y,\ \varphi(x,y)=\psi(x,y)$.

source.place: third paragraph, equality of regular maps into an affine variety
